doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
title: Woody Herman, Eddie Sauter and experimental writers
summary: Mandel contrasts Woody's tolerance for experiment with Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman's use of Eddie Sauter, and says he never got to know Sauter.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: esoterically too, which is why he and Woody never really hit it off. I mean they probably hit it off as people but, you know, we were all much more interested in experimenting then. And Woody allowed you to do things but if stuff got too linear and too… that’s why Woody and Eddie Sauter never hit it off, whereas Artie and Eddie Sauter did. The strangest thing was Benny and Eddie Sauter but that was kind of shotgun wedding, it just so happened that it was Benny's new band in 19… when was it?
Yeah I’d say ‘41, ‘42, the Lou McGarity band that Peggy Lee came into and Mel Powell and it was just a good atmosphere and they gave Sauter a lot of support.
Did you get to know Eddie at all?
Never got to know Eddie and I was always such an admirer of his, he was wonderful.
I did, I interviewed him for this program 15 years ago.
I think I met him once through Manny Albam but I was shy you know, and it was just in passing, I never really got to sit down and talk to Eddie.
You two would have enjoyed that, you know, you were kindred spirits.
I’ll tell you more about that on our own time.
But take my word for it.
Listen anybody who wrote like that… really quite something.
